It also does not connect well to the accompanying threat and memory items, which are clearly organized around combat/civilian danger cues rather than intimate-relationship themes.

vignette:
David, a 21-year-old social ministry worker, sought help after months of struggling to reconcile his present life with the indelible mark left by his time as a relief worker overseas. He recounted a harrowing incident from a year prior, where his humanitarian convoy, deep within a war zone, was ambushed by a militant group. He remembered the sudden, aggressive confrontation, the terrifying sight of armed men in military fatigues, and the deafening, enraged shouting in Arabic that echoed through the confined space of their vehicle. He had seen the terror in the eyes of his colleagues, certain that their lives were about to end, and the memory of that moment remained horrifyingly vivid.

Upon returning home and attempting to resume his life with his wife, David found that the world felt fundamentally altered. He struggled to talk about the event, finding that simply talking about the event as a trigger would immediately bring back the same terror he felt at the time, plunging him back into the chaos. The experience felt so extreme, so beyond the bounds of normal human experience, that he often found himself questioning if the story felt unreal, almost as though it couldn't possibly have happened to him. This profound sense of disbelief, paradoxically coupled with an overwhelming emotional vividness, made it difficult for him to process.

As weeks turned into months, David found himself caught in a tightening spiral. Conversations at work, even innocent discussions about current affairs or geopolitical tensions, if they touched upon military topics, could instantly activate a pervasive sense of dread. These triggers would cause the memory to feel like it was happening right now rather than something that was over, overwhelming him with a sense of immediate danger. In response, David developed several maladaptive strategies to cope; he would often delay sleep, staying up until very late, convinced that if he just stayed awake long enough, he could somehow prevent the vivid, terrifying flashbacks from taking hold. The constant re-experiencing of the event made him ruminate endlessly about how it could have been prevented, replaying scenarios in his mind in a futile attempt to find an escape route that never existed, a mental exercise that only kept the memory feeling present and raw.

This constant internal vigilance had tangible effects on his perception of the world. The persistent feeling that the memory was happening right now left him in a perpetual state of alert, particularly at night, leading him to wake during the night to check whether he was safe. This constant internal re-experiencing made him hyper-attuned to potential threats, transforming innocuous stimuli like sudden movements by others or the sight of strangers approaching into immediate, potent triggers. This internal sense of threat soon extended outwards. While working in the diverse community his ministry served, sudden movements by others would put him immediately on guard, his body tensing, ready to react. Even in ordinary situations, he now felt a deep threat from strangers approaching him, his mind instantly jumping to worst-case scenarios, a direct consequence of the ever-present, vivid memory of the ambush. This pervasive sense of threat also made him acutely sensitive to anything that might remind him of the past, amplifying the power of military topics or any sudden, loud shouting in Arabic to trigger intense anxiety.

The cycle continued to tighten. The constant state of threat, both internal and external, further distorted his perception of reality, making the memory feel even more present and impossible to escape. He found that the more he felt threatened, the more easily he was triggered, creating a feedback loop where the threat made him more vigilant, which in turn made him more susceptible to triggers. His attempts to manage this overwhelming internal landscape through maladaptive strategies, particularly his endless rumination about prevention, paradoxically kept the memory feeling present and difficult to integrate as something truly in the past. This exhausting internal battle, combined with the constant fear, led David to start avoiding situations that might make him feel happy or hopeful, believing that any moment of joy would only make him more vulnerable to the inevitable return of terror. His marriage, once a source of comfort, was now strained by his withdrawal, his sleepless nights, and his inability to fully engage with life. David sought help, exhausted and isolated, desperately hoping to find a way out of the prison his own mind had become.
